Coastal depositional systems – beach dynamics

  • November 8, 2026
  • 11:43 am
  • No Comments
  • 85

Beaches are a dynamic part of coastal systems

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 12:31
Instaread

The coastal realm is generally defined as the zone extending from the nearshore, commonly defined by the seaward limit of wave break or the point where waves significantly impact on the sea floor, to the inland limits of tidal reach by spring tides. Narrow coastal zones are typically bound by steep topography, particularly where sea cliffs plunge directly into the briny maelstrom. Much broader coastal zones include those that extend across sabkhas (flooded only by spring tides and storm surges), the landward margins of lagoons and barrier-coastal dune complexes, the tidal limits of estuaries and tidal channels, and tidal reach across delta plains. Coastal regions also support diverse ecosystems ranging from salt marshes and mangrove forests to coral reefs.

Beaches are the interface separating fully aquatic environments (marine and lacustrine) from terrestrial and atmospheric environments. Beaches are some of the most dynamic places on Earth, subjected to a never-ending procession of waves, and in marine settings, tides. They are forever changing which means they have spatial and temporal significance.

The processes that shape beaches

Beaches are relatively narrow strips of sediment between low and high tide limits; the sediment prism can extend into the backshore that is accessed by storm surges, and may also extend beyond the low tide limit. Beaches are moulded by physical processes associated with wind, waves and tides, longshore currents, sediment supply, and changing sea levels. Animal and plant biotas can also influence the character of a beach; precipitation of minerals like calcium carbonate can produce a protective armour (beachrock).

Wave dynamics

All beaches are moulded by waves. Surface waves are generated by wind shear across the water surface. Waves represent a disturbance in the equilibrium between water and atmosphere – gravity forces act to restore equilibrium (hence they are also called gravity waves). The amplitude and frequency of waves depends on the magnitude of the shear forces, and the duration and distance over which the wind blows. Open coasts with relatively unlimited fetch are typically subjected to relentless attack by energetic, long-period waves. Significantly lower energy, short period waves tend to lap the shores of protected harbours and lagoons. Such contrasts in wave energy across a beach are commonly reflected in sediment texture and composition, for example coarse versus fine grained, grain size sorting, the proportion of silt and mud, or the composition of invertebrate bioclasts.

Surface waves are energy pulses; there is no transfer of water mass in the direction of wave propagation. Instead, water particles beneath waves have a circular or elliptical orbital motion; the larger orbitals occurring immediately below the wave crest, decreasing in size to zero orbital motion at a depth that equates to about half the wavelength. In deep water, waves do not interact with the sea floor – they are referred to as deep-water waves, the speed of which depends only on the ratio of wavelength to wave period. Deep-water waves occur where water depth is greater than half the wavelength. Ocean waves beyond the nearshore are deep water waves.

As waves approach the coast, the wave orbitals begin to encounter the sea floor (referred to as wavebase or fairweather wavebase). The outer depth limit of wave-base is about half the wavelength. At these depths, loose sediment can be moved by the wave orbitals. Some energy is transferred to the sea floor and wave speed decreases, but to conserve energy the height, or wave amplitude must also increase. As you can see in the diagram, the orbitals also flatten. At this stage, the waves have become shallow-water waves. The depth to wavebase will change during seasonal variations in wave climate; storm waves tend to be longer wavelengths such that storm wavebase occurs in deeper water.

Wave energy is dampened by interaction with the sea floor. To conserve momentum, waves begin to increase in amplitude and steepness until they break – the region of wave break is called the surf zone. The breaking waves cause turbulence and move water masses onto the beach. Some of this energy is transferred to the loose, non-cohesive sediment in the surf zone that is carried across the beach by wave swash. Coarse materials like shells, pebbles, lumps of coral, or clumps of seaweed and plastic bottles are gradually pushed up the beach and left stranded at the high tide or spring tide limit. Storm waves will push this material farther up the beach or backshore.

Sediment budgets

The conditions of sediment supply to a beach or removal by erosion are generally in a state of constant change. Sediment budgets over the foreshore and beach are inextricably linked to sediment availability on the adjacent offshore shelf, and where present, coastal sand dunes. Sediment may also be supplied directly to the coast by rivers and delta distributary channels. Movement of sediment between any of these environments depends on seasonal and decadal changes in wave climate, wind and sea current directions and strengths; storms and tsunamis can drastically alter the balance between sediment supply and demand. Thus, beaches can be in a state of sediment balance, aggradation, or erosion depending on changes in budgetary constraints. The rate of change from constructional to erosional beaches and foreshores ranges from hours to decades.

Longshore currents

Surface wave crests tend to conform to or parallel the coastline during their approach. Deviation from this ideal condition means that waves impinge the surf zone and beach at an angle. The transfer of energy, instead of being directed normal to the beach, generates a current that is approximately parallel to the beach. Longshore currents can transport significant quantities of sediment (also called longshore drift) – they are commonly associated with sandspits and subtidal bars. Longshore currents are part of the sediment balancing act among beaches, coastal dunes, lagoons, and the offshore region.

Rip currents

Wave break in the surf zone pushes water onto the beach. Gravity then moves the water back down the beach slope to the surf zone. On all beaches, the return flow, or backwash, produces an undertow that flows beneath the incoming waves. Undertow occurs everywhere along a beach. Its influence is generally confined to the surf zone (and for the most part is not dangerous). 

Rip currents form when the returning seawater is diverted and focused by shallow holes and sand bars on the foreshore and beach, forming powerful, channel-like, seaward-directed currents that can extend beyond the surf zone. Rip currents, and the channels they erode, are a few 10s of metres wide. Flows as high as 4 m/second are common (hence the danger to swimmers). Rips can appear suddenly on any beach where there is appreciable wave activity – they also tend to migrate along the length of a beach.

Such powerful, channelized flows can move appreciable amounts of sediment from the lower part of a beach and foreshore to the offshore area, and as such are important contributors to the balance between coastal sediment supply.

Storm surges

The build-up of storm waves driven by strong onshore winds is accompanied by wave setup and the surge of water masses towards the coast. The effects are two-fold: local sea level rises temporarily, and breaking waves extend farther up the beach or supratidal zone. The beach itself can be completely remodeled where significant volumes of sand are eroded and moved offshore by return flows (see the example from New Zealand shown below). Artificial structures such as protective walls or boulder banks can be damaged.  Coastal dunes are also attacked by waves and sand redistributed – sand is commonly moved into adjacent lagoons and estuaries where coastal dunes have been breached. Storm waves that extend across hot, arid supratidal flats will erode microbial mats and reset local evaporite fluid chemistry (for example dissolution of halite).

Wind

In addition to promoting surface wave setup, wind is also responsible for mobilizing and redistributing sand in aeolian coastal dunes – much of this sand is sourced from the beach during low tide exposure. Coastal dune systems are dynamic – dunes and interdune flats are constantly being reshaped. They can also support vital ecosystems.

Coastal aeolian systems are an important determinant of coastal sediment budgets.

Depending on wind direction, sand can be returned to the beach or moved to lagoons and tidal channels where tidal exchange eventually moves it back to the foreshore and offshore shelf.

Tides

The Earth, Moon, and Sun are in a state of balance, determined by two opposing forces: gravity, and centrifugal forces. For the Earth-Moon system, the difference in forces between the side of Earth facing the Moon and the opposite side, produces a bulge in Earth’s ocean water masses. The tidal bulge is always aligned with the Moon, but because Earth rotates, the relative position of the bulge on Earth changes. The tidal bulge corresponds to high ocean tide – as Earth rotates, the bulge, and therefore high tide migrate, anticlockwise around land masses in the northern hemisphere, and clockwise in the southern hemisphere. The Sun also plays a role, manifested as changes in tidal range, from neap to spring tides. Intertidal zones and beaches owe their existence to the semidiurnal changes from high to low tides. (A king tide is a very high spring tide, caused by the advent of a spring tide during the Moon’s perigee, or closest approach).

High and low tides advance with time along ocean coasts. On a local scale, the tidal wave can be deflected, amplified, or weakened, depending on the shape of the coastline and variations in water depth. A classic example of tidal amplification is Fundy Bay, a narrow stretch of water between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia (eastern Canada).  Here tidal ranges of 17m are common, in marked contrast to those on the opposite coast (e.g. 2m tides in Halifax).

The variations in mean tidal range have been standardized, calculated as the difference between mean high and mean low tides:

Microtidal – Tidal range < 2m

Mesotidal – Tidal range 2 – 4 m

Macrotidal – > 4 m

Sea level

Sea level rises and falls with the passage of tides (daily), weather systems (seasonal) and decadal climate events like El Niňo.  These are short lived events. For example, the passage of low-pressure weather systems cause local sea levels to rise – Hurricane Katrina in 2005 produced a devastating surge about 8m above normal sea level. Sea level will also respond to ocean volume changes from grounded-ice melt and rising or falling seawater temperatures (steric changes).

Relative sea level also depends on changes in gravitational equilibrium that result from tectonic or sediment loading of the crust-mantle, the advance-retreat of ice sheets and ice caps, the densification of crust (particularly oceanic crust), and the response of the ocean floor to increasing or decreasing water volumes. The adjustment of the crust-mantle to addition or removal of loads, or isostasy, is geologically rapid – witness the uplift following the melting of ice caps during the last 7000-10000 years in regions like central Canada and Scandinavia.  For example, by dating deposits associated with raised beaches and stranded shore platforms, initial rates for postglacial uplift of southeastern Hudson Bay about 6500-7000 yr BP were as high as 6 m/100 years (e.g. Andrews and Falconer, 1969); uplift in this region continues at several millimetres/year.

Beaches and shorelines can also advance (regression) and retreat (transgression) because of autogenic changes in conditions such as sediment exchange between coastal dunes and the foreshore, or allogenic changes such as relatively long-term increases or decreases in basin subsidence, or external sediment supply accompanying changes in terrestrial uplift and denudation.

Beaches are never static. Sea level has risen and fallen countless times over the past 4.4 billion years, and with each rise or fall there has been a geographic shift in location (landward or seaward), and in some cases the kind of beach (coastal extent, steepness, composition).  We can decipher the trajectories of shoreline advance and retreat by tracking the sedimentological and paleontological changes in the stratigraphic record.

Some useful links

Nancy L. Jackson, 2017. Coastal Depositional Processes and Landforms. International Encyclopedia of Geography: People, the Earth, Environment and Technology.

Royal Geographical Society. Coasts: How will climate change impact on erosional processes and landforms in British waters? School resources.

Juan A. Morales, 2022. Coastal Geology. Springer-Nature.

Eric Bird, 2008. Coastal Geomorphology; An Introduction. Wiley & Sons. 448 p.

Robin Davidson-Arnott, 2019. Introduction to Coastal Processes and Geomorphology. Cambridge University Press.
